solution:
The torque on a magnetic dipole in a uniform field is \(\tau = mB\sin\theta\).
Here \(\tau = 4.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{J}\), \(B = 0.25\,\text{T}\) and \(\theta = 30^{\circ}\), so \(\sin\theta = 0.5\).
Rearranging, \(m = \dfrac{\tau}{B\sin\theta} = \dfrac{4.5 \times 10^{-2}}{0.25 \times 0.5} = \dfrac{4.5 \times 10^{-2}}{0.125}\).
\(m = 0.36\,\text{J T}^{-1}\) (equivalently \(0.36\,\text{A m}^{2}\)).

The potential energy of a magnetic dipole in a uniform field is \(U = -\mathbf{m}\cdot\mathbf{B} = -mB\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\mathbf{m}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\). \(U\) is least when \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\) and greatest when \(\theta = 180^{\circ}\), so those are the stable and unstable orientations respectively.
With \(m = 0.32\,\text{J T}^{-1}\) and \(B = 0.15\,\text{T}\), \(mB = 0.32 \times 0.15 = 0.048\,\text{J}\).
(a) Stable equilibrium: the magnetic moment is aligned with the field, \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\), and \(U = -mB = -4.8 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{J}\).
(b) Unstable equilibrium: the magnetic moment is anti-parallel to the field, \(\theta = 180^{\circ}\), and \(U = +mB = +4.8 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{J}\).

A current-carrying solenoid sets up field lines that emerge from one flat face and re-enter the other, and at axial distances large compared with its length its field is \(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^{3}}\) — the same form as the far axial field of a bar magnet. So the face the lines leave behaves as a north pole and the face they enter as a south pole, and the solenoid experiences a torque (but no net force) in a uniform field exactly as a bar magnet does.
Its magnetic moment is the sum of the moments of the \(N\) turns, \(m = NIA\).
\(m = 800 \times 3.0\,\text{A} \times 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}\)
\(m = 0.60\,\text{J T}^{-1}\) (equivalently \(0.60\,\text{A m}^{2}\)), directed along the axis of the solenoid from its south face to its north face.

[Textbook misprint, TWO of them, neither changing the value. (1) The stem says "the solenoid in Exercise 5.5", but Exercise 5.5 is a BAR MAGNET, not a solenoid — the intended target is Exercise 5.3. The book's own key proves it: Ex 5.3's solenoid has \(m = 0.60\,\text{J T}^{-1}\), which gives \(\tau = mB\sin\theta = 0.075\,\text{N m}\) — exactly the printed answer — while Ex 5.5's magnet (\(m = 1.5\)) would give \(0.1875\). A leftover from the pre-rationalisation numbering. (2) The key states that torque with the UNIT JOULE. Torque is measured in newton-metres; the key itself prints "N m" for the same quantity at Exercise 4.9 and "Nm" at 5.6(b). The magnitude \(7.5 \times 10^{-2}\) is correct.] The solenoid meant here is the 800-turn solenoid of Exercise 5.3, whose magnetic moment is \(m = NIA = 800 \times 3.0 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-4} = 0.60\,\text{J T}^{-1}\).
A uniform field exerts no net force on it, only a torque \(\tau = mB\sin\theta\).
With \(B = 0.25\,\text{T}\) and \(\theta = 30^{\circ}\),
\(\tau = 0.60 \times 0.25 \times 0.5\)
\(\tau = 7.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N m}\).

solution:
[Textbook misprint in the answer key (unit only): all four values agree with the answer below, but the key gives the torque in part (b)(i) as \(0.33\,\text{J}\). Torque is measured in newton-metres, not joules — the key prints "N m" correctly for the same quantity elsewhere. The same key entry also reads "the magnitude moment vector", a typo for MAGNETIC moment.] The work done by the external torque against the field equals the change in potential energy, \(W = U_{2} - U_{1} = mB(\cos\theta_{1} - \cos\theta_{2})\), since \(U = -mB\cos\theta\). The magnet starts aligned with the field, so \(\theta_{1} = 0^{\circ}\).
Here \(mB = 1.5 \times 0.22 = 0.33\,\text{J}\).
(a) (i) Turning to \(\theta_{2} = 90^{\circ}\): \(W = mB(1 - 0) = 0.33\,\text{J}\).
(ii) Turning to \(\theta_{2} = 180^{\circ}\): \(W = mB(1 - (-1)) = 2mB = 0.66\,\text{J}\).
(b) The torque is \(\tau = mB\sin\theta\) evaluated at the final orientation.
(i) At \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\): \(\tau = 1.5 \times 0.22 \times 1 = 0.33\,\text{N m}\).
(ii) At \(\theta = 180^{\circ}\): \(\tau = 1.5 \times 0.22 \times 0 = 0\).
So the work is \(0.33\,\text{J}\) and \(0.66\,\text{J}\), and the torque is \(0.33\,\text{N m}\) and \(0\), respectively.

(a) The magnetic moment of a closely wound solenoid is \(m = NIA\).
\(m = 2000 \times 4.0\,\text{A} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2} = 1.28\,\text{J T}^{-1}\) (i.e. \(1.28\,\text{A m}^{2}\)), directed along the axis of the solenoid.
(b) In a UNIFORM field the forces on the two ends are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero.
The torque is \(\tau = mB\sin\theta = 1.28 \times 7.5 \times 10^{-2} \times \sin 30^{\circ}\)
\(\tau = 1.28 \times 7.5 \times 10^{-2} \times 0.5 = 4.8 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N m}\), acting so as to turn the axis of the solenoid into alignment with the field.
Force \(= 0\); torque \(= 4.8 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N m}\).

For a short bar magnet at a distance \(r \gg l\), the axial and equatorial fields are
\(B_{A} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^{3}}\) and \(B_{E} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{r^{3}}\), with \(\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi} = 10^{-7}\,\text{T m A}^{-1}\).
Here \(m = 0.48\,\text{J T}^{-1}\) and \(r = 10\,\text{cm} = 0.10\,\text{m}\), so \(r^{3} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^{3}\).
(a) On the axis: \(B_{A} = 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{2 \times 0.48}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 9.6 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{T} = 0.96\,\text{G}\), directed along the axis parallel to the magnetic moment, i.e. in the S-N direction of the magnet.
(b) On the equatorial line: \(B_{E} = 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{0.48}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 4.8 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{T} = 0.48\,\text{G}\), directed anti-parallel to the magnetic moment, i.e. in the N-S direction.
